hints: Remember a conjugate pair contains the same two species linked by loss or gain of one $\text{H}^{+}$, so match each acid on the left with the base it becomes on the right.
walkthrough:
Picture what a conjugate pair means**
Think of an acid as a proton donor. When it gives away its $\text{H}^{+}$ it turns into its own conjugate base. The two forms differ by exactly one $\text{H}^{+}$ and nothing else.

Pair them up across the equation**
$\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ loses $\text{H}^{+}$ to become $\text{OH}^{-}$, so they are one pair. $\text{HNO}_{2}$ is formed when $\text{NO}_{2}^{-}$ gains $\text{H}^{+}$, so $\text{HNO}_{2}$ and $\text{NO}_{2}^{-}$ are the second pair.

Final answer: acid I $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ with conjugate base $\text{OH}^{-}$
acid II $\text{HNO}_{2}$ with conjugate base $\text{NO}_{2}^{-}$

hints: Draw $\text{CH}_{3}\text{NH}_{2}$ in your mind and focus on the nitrogen atom, what non-bonding electrons does it carry that carbon and hydrogen do not?
walkthrough:
See why nitrogen is special**
In $\text{CH}_{3}\text{NH}_{2}$ the nitrogen has three covalent bonds plus one lone pair. That lone pair is available and is the reactive centre.

Link the lone pair to basic behaviour**
A Bronsted-Lowry base accepts $\text{H}^{+}$. The lone pair on N can donate into the empty orbital of $\text{H}^{+}$ from water, forming a dative bond to give $\text{CH}_{3}\text{NH}_{3}^{+}$ and $\text{OH}^{-}$.
Final answer: The N atom in $\text{CH}_{3}\text{NH}_{2}$ has a lone pair which can be donated to / accept $\text{H}^{+}$ to form a dative bond.

hints: If water is the base here, decide which species donates the proton and what water becomes after it gains that $\text{H}^{+}$.
walkthrough:
Assign the roles**
$\text{CH}_{3}\text{COOH}$ is the familiar acid, so it donates $\text{H}^{+}$. Water must therefore act as the base and accept $\text{H}^{+}$.

Write the proton transfer**
Water gains $\text{H}^{+}$ to become $\text{H}_{3}\text{O}^{+}$, while $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COOH}$ loses $\text{H}^{+}$ to become $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COO}^{-}$: $$\text{H}_{2}\text{O} + \text{CH}_{3}\text{COOH} \rightarrow \text{H}_{3}\text{O}^{+} + \text{CH}_{3}\text{COO}^{-}$$

hints: Start from $K_{c}$ for $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^{+}(aq) + \text{OH}^{-}(aq)$ and recall why the concentration of pure liquid water is omitted.
walkthrough:
Build the equilibrium expression**
For $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^{+}(aq) + \text{OH}^{-}(aq)$ the $K_{c}$ expression would include $[\text{H}_{2}\text{O}]$ in the denominator.

Simplify for a pure liquid**
$[\text{H}_{2}\text{O}(l)]$ is effectively constant and is absorbed into the constant, leaving the ionic product: $$K_{w} = [\text{H}^{+}][\text{OH}^{-}]$$

hints: Look carefully at Fig. 2.1, does $K_{w}$ rise or fall as temperature rises, and what does that tell you about whether more water dissociates on heating?
walkthrough:
Read the graph**
Fig. 2.1 shows $K_{w}$ increasing steadily from near zero at $0^{\circ}\text{C}$ to about $5.4 \times 10^{-14}$ at $50^{\circ}\text{C}$. A larger $K_{w}$ means more $\text{H}^{+}$ and $\text{OH}^{-}$, so dissociation increases.

Apply Le Chatelier thinking**
Increasing temperature shifts equilibrium in the endothermic direction. Since heating favours more dissociation, the forward dissociation must absorb heat, so it is endothermic.
Final answer: Endothermic, as $K_{w}$ increases with temperature so equilibrium moves to the right with increased dissociation on heating.

hints: Recall that neutral means $[\text{H}^{+}] = [\text{OH}^{-}]$, so use the $K_{w}$ value at $30^{\circ}\text{C}$ from Fig. 2.1 to find the neutral $[\text{H}^{+}]$.
Compare the given pH 7.00 with the neutral pH you calculate, or compare $[\text{H}^{+}]$ with $[\text{OH}^{-}]$, to decide if the solution has excess $\text{OH}^{-}$.
walkthrough:
Find neutral pH at $30^{\circ}\text{C}$**
From Fig. 2.1, $K_{w} = 1.50 \times 10^{-14}$ at $30^{\circ}\text{C}$. In a neutral solution $[\text{H}^{+}] = [\text{OH}^{-}]$, so: $$K_{w} = [\text{H}^{+}]^{2} = 1.50 \times 10^{-14}$$ $$\text{pH}_{neutral} = -0.5\log(1.50 \times 10^{-14}) = 6.91$$ Neutral is no longer 7.00 when warm.

Compare pH 7.00 to neutral**
A solution of pH 7.00 has $[\text{H}^{+}] = 1.00 \times 10^{-7}$ $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$, giving $[\text{OH}^{-}] = 1.50 \times 10^{-14}/10^{-7.00} = 1.50 \times 10^{-7}$ $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$. Since $[\text{OH}^{-}] > [\text{H}^{+}]$, or pH 7.00 is greater than the neutral pH of 6.91, the solution is alkaline.

Final answer: At $30^{\circ}\text{C}$, $K_{w} = 1.50 \times 10^{-14} = [\text{H}^{+}]^{2}$ in neutral solution, so neutral pH $= -0.5\log(1.50 \times 10^{-14}) = 6.91$. pH 7.00 is above neutral pH so $[\text{OH}^{-}] > [\text{H}^{+}]$, hence alkaline.

hints: Compare how freely water molecules can move and arrange themselves in a rigid ice lattice versus in mobile liquid water.
walkthrough:
Picture the particles**
In ice, $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ molecules are locked in a fixed hydrogen bonded lattice and can only vibrate. In liquid water the hydrogen bonds are constantly breaking and reforming, so molecules can translate and rotate.

Link movement to entropy**
More freedom of movement means more possible arrangements of particles and of energy quanta, so disorder is higher. That is why $S^{\ominus}$ rises from $+48.0$ to $+70.1$ $\text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$ on melting.
Final answer: $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}(l)$ has greater disorder / more ways of arranging particles and energy than $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}(s)$.

hints: Think about the huge increase in volume and freedom when molecules escape from close contact in the liquid to widely spaced motion in the gas.
walkthrough:
Picture boiling**
Boiling completely separates molecules that were still close together in the liquid. Gas molecules occupy a volume roughly a thousand times larger and move randomly at high speed.

Explain the big jump**
That enormous increase in freedom gives vastly more possible positions and energy distributions, so entropy jumps sharply from $+70.1$ to $+188.7$ $\text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$, far larger than the small increase on melting.
Final answer: $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}(g)$ has much greater disorder / many more ways of arranging particles and energy than $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}(l)$.

hints: At the melting point solid and liquid are in equilibrium, so start from $\Delta G = 0 = \Delta H - T\Delta S$ and work out $\Delta S$ for melting from Table 2.1.
walkthrough:
Set the equilibrium condition**
At the melting point $\Delta G = 0$, so $0 = \Delta H - T\Delta S$ and $T = \Delta H / \Delta S$. Convert $\Delta H$ to joules: $+6.03$ $\text{kJ mol}^{-1} = 6030$ $\text{J mol}^{-1}$.

Substitute and calculate**
$$\Delta S = 70.1 - 48.0 = +22.1 \text{ J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$$ $$T = 6030 / 22.1 = 272.9 \text{ K} \approx 273 \text{ K}$$ which is $0^{\circ}\text{C}$, confirming the melting point of ice.
Final answer: $\Delta S = 70.1 - 48.0 = +22.1$ $\text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$, $T = \Delta H/\Delta S = 6030/22.1 = 273$ K $= 0^{\circ}\text{C}$

hints: Identify which half equation is reduction at the cathode (more positive $E^{\ominus}$) and which is reversed as oxidation, then subtract accordingly.
walkthrough:
Pick cathode and anode**
The oxygen half cell with $E^{\ominus} = +0.40$ V is the cathode (reduction). The zinc half cell with $E^{\ominus} = -1.22$ V is the anode (oxidation).

Calculate**
$$E^{\ominus}_{cell} = E^{\ominus}_{cathode} - E^{\ominus}_{anode} = +0.40 - (-1.22) = +1.62 \text{ V}$$
Final answer: $E^{\ominus}_{cell} = +0.40 - (-1.22) = +1.62$ V

hints: Convert pH 11 to $[\text{H}^{+}]$ then to $[\text{OH}^{-}]$ using $K_{w} = 10^{-14}$, paying attention to powers of ten.
Read $z$ as the number of electrons in the cathode half equation ($2e^{-}$) and substitute $[\text{OH}^{-}]$ into $E = 0.40 - (0.059/z)\log([\text{OH}^{-}]^{2})$.
walkthrough:
Apply the Nernst equation**
The cathode reaction uses $z = 2$ electrons: $$E = 0.40 - (0.059/2)\log([\text{OH}^{-}]^{2})$$ $$E = 0.40 - 0.5 \times 0.059 \times \log(1.0 \times 10^{-3})^{2}$$ $$E = 0.40 - 0.5 \times 0.059 \times (-6) = 0.40 + 0.177 = +0.577 \text{ V}$$ Higher $[\text{OH}^{-}]$ might be expected to lower $E$, but here the log term is negative so $E$ rises above $+0.40$ V.
